A0225.explanation: Landlords may only charge one month's rent as a security deposit for unfurnished and furnished units, starting July 1, 2024.

Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total can charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons.
Landlords must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy to identify any items that need repair or cleaning.
All or any remaining portion of a security deposit must be returned within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant, with an itemized statement of deductions if applicable.
Starting January 1, 2025, landlords must provide proof that necessary repairs were completed when making deductions from a security deposit.

Housing providers may not consider certain categories of criminal history (arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged records, juvenile records) when screening applicants, and may not impose blanket bans on applicants with any criminal history.
Housing providers may not impose conditions that discriminate against households with children, including charging higher security deposits to families with children.
Housing providers may not charge higher security deposits or apply different terms based on an applicant's or tenant's source of income, such as Section 8 vouchers.
Tenants with service animals or emotional-support animals cannot be charged pet deposits or pet rent for those animals.

It is unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, or to coerce another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by a common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in California.

After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which must be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. Just cause includes at-fault reasons (e.g., nonpayment of rent, lease violations, nuisance, waste, criminal activity) and no-fault reasons (e.g., owner move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate, demolition or substantial remodel), with relocation assistance or rent waiver required for no-fault terminations.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, based on the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months, with no more than two increments over that period.
If the same tenant remains in occupancy over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period.

For a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the owner may establish the initial rental rate without the cap applying; the cap applies only to subsequent increases after that initial rate is set.

The rent cap does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories, housing subject to stricter local rent control, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome), certain single-family/condo properties meeting ownership and notice conditions, and owner-occupied duplexes.
An owner shall provide notice of any rent increase under subdivision (a) to each tenant in accordance with Section 827.
This section shall remain in effect until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.
A landlord shall not demand or receive security in an amount exceeding one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent, except as otherwise provided.
The one month's rent security deposit cap does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months' rent if the lease term is six months or longer.
Service Member Higher Security Disclosure is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

A landlord who is a natural person or LLC of natural persons owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units total may charge up to two months' rent as security deposit, unless the tenant is a service member.
Any security deposit shall be held by the landlord for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to the security has priority over any creditor of the landlord.
The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy, or for ordinary wear and tear.

The landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the right to request an initial inspection before move-out and must conduct the inspection upon tenant request, giving at least 48 hours' notice, to allow the tenant to remedy deficiencies before final deductions.
Photographs Required at Move-In is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated, the landlord shall furnish the tenant an itemized statement of deductions and return any remaining portion of the security deposit.
The landlord need not provide documentation for deductions if the deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed $125.

The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord of the security deposit in violation of this section may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security deposit as 'nonrefundable.'
Cap on Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Conditions for Charging Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

Landlords may not use a financial or income standard in rental housing that fails to account for the aggregate income of unmarried persons residing together on the same basis as married persons residing together.

When there is a government rent subsidy, landlords may not use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for rental housing that is not based on the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant.

When there is a government rent subsidy, a landlord using a person's credit history as part of the application process must offer the applicant the option to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their reasonable ability to pay the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant, such as government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements, and must reasonably consider that evidence in lieu of credit history.

If an applicant elects to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their ability to pay, the housing provider must provide the applicant reasonable time to respond with that alternative evidence and reasonably consider that alternative evidence in lieu of the person's credit history in determining whether to offer the rental accommodation to the applicant.

Annual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region, or 10%, whichever is lower, for buildings older than 15 years not otherwise exempt.
From August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable rent increase under AB 1482 is 8.9%.
State law requires landlords to provide 30 days' written advance notice of rent increases of less than 10%.
Protects residents with arrest or conviction history from discrimination in affordable housing decisions.

In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction, and the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute just cause.

The landlord also needs a just cause reason to take away or remove access to certain housing services, including but not limited to garage facilities, parking facilities, driveways, storage spaces, and laundry rooms.

Some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limitations of the Ordinance, including newly constructed rental units with Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 and tenancies eligible for increases under Costa-Hawkins, are still subject to just cause eviction requirements.
For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is capped at 1.6%.

Prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco; allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action for violations.

The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions lasting less than 20 days is governed by state law rather than the local Rent Ordinance provision covering longer displacements.
Landlords subject to the San Francisco Rent Ordinance may increase rent by no more than 1.6% during the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
Landlords must pay tenants interest on security deposits at a rate of 4.2% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.

Landlords must pay relocation benefits to tenants evicted for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal of a unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation.
Landlords who evict tenants under the Ellis Act must pay relocation payments as set forth in the Rent Ordinance.
For temporary capital improvement evictions resulting in displacement of less than 20 days, relocation payments are governed by state law rather than the Rent Ordinance.

A0226.explanation: Housing providers receiving DND funding/land or with BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy units may not impose a blanket policy denying housing to anyone with arrests or convictions; applicants must be considered case-by-case.

Agents may not consider arrests without conviction, convictions subject to judicial relief, juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old when determining housing eligibility or eviction, except where there is a direct relationship to safety risk.
A conviction more than 5 years old generally may not be considered in tenant selection decisions, absent a direct relationship to safety risk.
Agents agree not to use an applicant's credit score to approve or deny housing applications.
Property managers may only use credit history in lieu of rental history to determine ability to pay rent when rental history is not available.
The lack of credit history, as opposed to poor credit history, is not sufficient justification to reject an applicant.

Boston Tenant Eviction Protections Authorization is pending and is not in force.

All landlords planning to end a tenancy agreement must provide the tenant with a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources at the same time as the Notice to Quit or Notice of non-renewal of lease, and must notify the City via an online form with tenant contact information and a copy of the notice.
Landlords who fail to submit the Notice to Quit/Non-renewal of Lease Submission Verification Form through the online portal may be fined up to $300 per day.
Violations of the Housing Stability Notification Act are enforced by Inspectional Services, with a warning for the first offense and a $300 per day fine for the second and subsequent offenses.
If a landlord violates the Housing Stability Notification Act, the violation does not halt the eviction process.
Violations of the HSNA are enforced by the Inspectional Services Department, with a warning for a first offense and a $300 per day fine for subsequent offenses.

Cities and towns may not enact, maintain, or enforce rent control of any kind, except that a city or town may accept this chapter and adopt rent control regulation that meets specific conditions, including voluntary compliance after six months, exclusions for small property owners and higher-rent units, and a requirement that the municipality compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and controlled rent.

After six months from the initial adoption of rent control regulation by a city or town, compliance by property owners is entirely voluntary, and property of an owner declining to participate is unaffected by the regulation.

Local rent control regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties from regulation, and may not apply to rental units owned by an owner with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control regulation must compensate owners of rent controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its rent controlled rent, with such compensation paid from the municipality's general funds so that the cost is borne by all taxpayers rather than only the owners of regulated units.

Landlords and persons furnishing rental accommodations or credit may not discriminate against a prospective or current tenant because that person receives federal, state, or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or receives federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, nor may they discriminate because of any requirement of such assistance or subsidy program.

A landlord may terminate a tenancy for nonpayment of rent by giving fourteen days' written notice to quit, unless the tenant pays or tenders all rent due, with interest and costs, before the answer is due in a possession action.

If nonpayment of rent was caused by delay in a government subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days to notify the agency, and must treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent, interest, and costs are tendered within that time.

Tenancies at will may be terminated by either party with three months' written notice, or if rent is paid at intervals of less than three months, notice equal to the payment interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment of rent, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient, unless the tenant has not received similar notice in the preceding twelve months, in which case the tenant may cure by paying all rent due within ten days of receipt of the notice. Notices for nonpayment must include a statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent due, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient to terminate a tenancy at will, unless the tenant has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months and pays or tenders the full amount of rent due within ten days after receipt of the notice.

Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent must contain a specific notification informing the tenant of their right to prevent termination by paying the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt, if they have not received such a notice within the preceding twelve months.

If a notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent fails to contain the required statutory notification, the tenant's time to pay or tender rent is extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises.

If neglect or refusal to pay rent was caused by a delay in mailing or delivery of a subsistence or rental payment by a government entity, the court must continue the hearing for at least seven days to notify the appropriate agency, and shall treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to the landlord within that time.
A lessor may not require a security deposit exceeding the first month's rent, provided the deposit is held as required and a statement of condition is given to the tenant.

No lessor may require a tenant to pay more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to first month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock at or prior to commencement of tenancy.
Security deposits must be held in a separate, interest-bearing bank account located within the Commonwealth, beyond the reach of the lessor's creditors.
A lessor holding a security deposit for one year or longer must pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser amount actually earned) to the tenant annually.
The lessor must return the security deposit or balance thereof to the tenant within thirty days after termination of occupancy, subject to allowed deductions.

A lessor accepting a security deposit must furnish the tenant a written statement of the present condition of the premises, including a comprehensive listing of any existing damage, within specified timeframes.

A lessor forfeits the right to retain any portion of a security deposit if they fail to deposit funds properly, fail to provide itemized damage list, use conflicting lease provisions, fail to transfer deposit to successor, or fail to timely return the deposit.
If a lessor fails to comply with certain security deposit requirements, the tenant shall be awarded treble damages plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit Option is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
A security deposit continues to be the property of the tenant, cannot be commingled with lessor's assets, and is not subject to claims of the lessor's creditors.

No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those explicitly set forth in the statute, such as unpaid rent, unpaid tax escalation amounts, or damage caused by the tenant.
Any lease provision conflicting with the security deposit statute, or any tenant waiver of its provisions, is void and unenforceable as against public policy.

Landlords are prohibited from taking reprisals against tenants for reporting code violations, joining tenant unions, or exercising legal rights; receipt of a termination notice, rent increase, or substantial alteration of tenancy terms within six months of protected tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of independent justification; any lease waiver of this protection is void.
Broker/Finder Fee Payment Restriction for Rental Housing is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

No person may engage in the business of finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee unless that person is a licensed broker or salesman as defined under section 87PP of chapter 112.

A landlord's written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent must be accompanied by a form containing documentation of repayment agreements, information on rental assistance programs, applicable court rules/orders on summary process, and relevant legal restrictions on evictions, along with a prominent statement informing the tenant that the notice is not an eviction and that only a court order can force them to leave. Courts may not accept eviction filings for nonpayment of rent without proof of delivery of this form.

The notice form must prominently display a statement informing tenants that a notice to quit is not an eviction, that they do not need to immediately leave, that they are entitled to a legal proceeding to defend against the eviction, and that only a court order can force them to leave.

No court with jurisdiction over summary process actions, including the Boston municipal court department, may accept for filing a writ, summons, or complaint in an eviction for nonpayment of rent for a residential dwelling unit without proof of delivery of the required notice-to-quit form.

A0227.explanation: A housing provider shall not require an applicant to complete any housing application that includes any inquiries regarding an applicant's criminal record prior to the provision of a conditional offer, nor make any oral or written inquiry regarding an applicant's criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

A housing provider shall not, either before or after the issuance of a conditional offer, evaluate an applicant based on arrests or charges that have not resulted in a criminal conviction, expunged convictions, convictions erased through executive pardon, vacated and otherwise legally nullified convictions, juvenile adjudications of delinquency, and records that have been sealed.

After a conditional offer, a housing provider may only consider certain serious convictions, or indictable offenses within specified lookback periods: six years for first-degree offenses, four years for second- or third-degree offenses, and one year for fourth-degree offenses.

Prior to accepting any application fee, a housing provider shall disclose in writing to the applicant whether the eligibility criteria include review of criminal history and a statement regarding the applicant's right to provide evidence of inaccuracies or rehabilitation.
A housing provider shall not require an applicant to submit to a drug or alcohol test, or request the applicant's consent to obtain information from a drug abuse treatment facility.

A housing provider shall not knowingly or purposefully publish, or cause to be published, any housing advertisement that explicitly provides that the housing provider will not consider any applicant who has been arrested or convicted of one or more crimes or offenses, with limited exceptions.
Residential Rental Property Application Fee Cap is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Penalties for Violating Application Fee Cap is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
New Jersey has no state law establishing, governing, or controlling rents; municipalities may pass ordinances establishing rent control or rent leveling, enforced by locally created boards.
Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from any local rent control ordinances for a period of 30 years following completion of construction of the building.

A landlord cannot raise rent mid-lease; the old lease must be terminated and a new lease offered with the increased rent, and the increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
A landlord may recover possession of a dwelling unit used as a residence only by consent of the tenants or through the legal process of eviction, and must have good cause to evict a tenant.
The maximum security deposit a landlord may collect cannot be more than one and one-half times one month's rent.
Any additional yearly security deposit increase may not exceed 10% of the current security deposit.
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant.

The interest or earnings paid on the security deposit belongs to the tenant and must be paid to the tenant in cash or credited toward rent due on the renewal or anniversary of the lease, or on January 31 if proper written notice has been given.

If a landlord fails to return the security deposit within 30 days or the tenant disagrees with deductions, the tenant may sue for double the amount wrongfully withheld, plus court costs and attorney's fees.
Landlords may charge the tenant for the cost of a credit report and may also request reasonable rental application fees or employment verification.

If a tenant's application is denied due to their credit report, the landlord must provide the tenant with the name, address, and telephone number of the credit reporting or screening agency that supplied the negative report.
Landlords cannot deny housing to a lawful recipient of a Section 8 HUD voucher or other lawful source of income or rent payment.

After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which must be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, based on the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months, with no more than two increments over that period.
If the same tenant remains in occupancy over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period.

For a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the owner may establish the initial rental rate without the cap applying; the cap applies only to subsequent increases after that initial rate is set.

The rent cap does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories, housing subject to stricter local rent control, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome), certain single-family/condo properties meeting ownership and notice conditions, and owner-occupied duplexes.

Cities and towns may not enact, maintain, or enforce rent control of any kind, except that a city or town may accept this chapter and adopt rent control regulation that meets specific conditions, including voluntary compliance after six months, exclusions for small property owners and higher-rent units, and a requirement that the municipality compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and controlled rent.

After six months from the initial adoption of rent control regulation by a city or town, compliance by property owners is entirely voluntary, and property of an owner declining to participate is unaffected by the regulation.

Local rent control regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties from regulation, and may not apply to rental units owned by an owner with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control regulation must compensate owners of rent controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its rent controlled rent, with such compensation paid from the municipality's general funds so that the cost is borne by all taxpayers rather than only the owners of regulated units.

Landlords and persons furnishing rental accommodations or credit may not discriminate against a prospective or current tenant because that person receives federal, state, or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or receives federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, nor may they discriminate because of any requirement of such assistance or subsidy program.

A landlord may terminate a tenancy for nonpayment of rent by giving fourteen days' written notice to quit, unless the tenant pays or tenders all rent due, with interest and costs, before the answer is due in a possession action.

If nonpayment of rent was caused by delay in a government subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days to notify the agency, and must treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent, interest, and costs are tendered within that time.

Tenancies at will may be terminated by either party with three months' written notice, or if rent is paid at intervals of less than three months, notice equal to the payment interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment of rent, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient, unless the tenant has not received similar notice in the preceding twelve months, in which case the tenant may cure by paying all rent due within ten days of receipt of the notice. Notices for nonpayment must include a statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent due, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient to terminate a tenancy at will, unless the tenant has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months and pays or tenders the full amount of rent due within ten days after receipt of the notice.

Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent must contain a specific notification informing the tenant of their right to prevent termination by paying the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt, if they have not received such a notice within the preceding twelve months.

If a notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent fails to contain the required statutory notification, the tenant's time to pay or tender rent is extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises.

If neglect or refusal to pay rent was caused by a delay in mailing or delivery of a subsistence or rental payment by a government entity, the court must continue the hearing for at least seven days to notify the appropriate agency, and shall treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to the landlord within that time.
A lessor may not require a security deposit exceeding the first month's rent, provided the deposit is held as required and a statement of condition is given to the tenant.

No lessor may require a tenant to pay more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to first month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock at or prior to commencement of tenancy.
Security deposits must be held in a separate, interest-bearing bank account located within the Commonwealth, beyond the reach of the lessor's creditors.
A lessor holding a security deposit for one year or longer must pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser amount actually earned) to the tenant annually.
The lessor must return the security deposit or balance thereof to the tenant within thirty days after termination of occupancy, subject to allowed deductions.

A lessor accepting a security deposit must furnish the tenant a written statement of the present condition of the premises, including a comprehensive listing of any existing damage, within specified timeframes.

A lessor forfeits the right to retain any portion of a security deposit if they fail to deposit funds properly, fail to provide itemized damage list, use conflicting lease provisions, fail to transfer deposit to successor, or fail to timely return the deposit.
If a lessor fails to comply with certain security deposit requirements, the tenant shall be awarded treble damages plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit Option is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
A security deposit continues to be the property of the tenant, cannot be commingled with lessor's assets, and is not subject to claims of the lessor's creditors.

No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those explicitly set forth in the statute, such as unpaid rent, unpaid tax escalation amounts, or damage caused by the tenant.
Any lease provision conflicting with the security deposit statute, or any tenant waiver of its provisions, is void and unenforceable as against public policy.

Landlords are prohibited from taking reprisals against tenants for reporting code violations, joining tenant unions, or exercising legal rights; receipt of a termination notice, rent increase, or substantial alteration of tenancy terms within six months of protected tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of independent justification; any lease waiver of this protection is void.

Courts may not accept eviction filings for nonpayment of rent without proof of delivery of this form.

The notice form must prominently display a statement informing tenants that a notice to quit is not an eviction, that they do not need to immediately leave, that they are entitled to a legal proceeding to defend against the eviction, and that only a court order can force them to leave.

No court with jurisdiction over summary process actions, including the Boston municipal court department, may accept for filing a writ, summons, or complaint in an eviction for nonpayment of rent for a residential dwelling unit without proof of delivery of the required notice-to-quit form.

Landlords must pay tenants interest on security deposits at a rate of 4.2% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.

Landlords must pay relocation benefits to tenants evicted for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal of a unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation.

Cities and towns may not enact, maintain, or enforce rent control of any kind, except that a city or town may accept this chapter and adopt rent control regulation that meets specific conditions, including voluntary compliance after six months, exclusions for small property owners and higher-rent units, and a requirement that the municipality compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and controlled rent.

After six months from the initial adoption of rent control regulation by a city or town, compliance by property owners is entirely voluntary, and property of an owner declining to participate is unaffected by the regulation.

Local rent control regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties from regulation, and may not apply to rental units owned by an owner with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control regulation must compensate owners of rent controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its rent controlled rent, with such compensation paid from the municipality's general funds so that the cost is borne by all taxpayers rather than only the owners of regulated units.

Landlords and persons furnishing rental accommodations or credit may not discriminate against a prospective or current tenant because that person receives federal, state, or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or receives federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, nor may they discriminate because of any requirement of such assistance or subsidy program.

A landlord may terminate a tenancy for nonpayment of rent by giving fourteen days' written notice to quit, unless the tenant pays or tenders all rent due, with interest and costs, before the answer is due in a possession action.

If nonpayment of rent was caused by delay in a government subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days to notify the agency, and must treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent, interest, and costs are tendered within that time.

Tenancies at will may be terminated by either party with three months' written notice, or if rent is paid at intervals of less than three months, notice equal to the payment interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment of rent, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient, unless the tenant has not received similar notice in the preceding twelve months, in which case the tenant may cure by paying all rent due within ten days of receipt of the notice. Notices for nonpayment must include a statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent due, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient to terminate a tenancy at will, unless the tenant has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months and pays or tenders the full amount of rent due within ten days after receipt of the notice.

Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent must contain a specific notification informing the tenant of their right to prevent termination by paying the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt, if they have not received such a notice within the preceding twelve months.

If a notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent fails to contain the required statutory notification, the tenant's time to pay or tender rent is extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises.

If neglect or refusal to pay rent was caused by a delay in mailing or delivery of a subsistence or rental payment by a government entity, the court must continue the hearing for at least seven days to notify the appropriate agency, and shall treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to the landlord within that time.
A lessor may not require a security deposit exceeding the first month's rent, provided the deposit is held as required and a statement of condition is given to the tenant.

No lessor may require a tenant to pay more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to first month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock at or prior to commencement of tenancy.
Security deposits must be held in a separate, interest-bearing bank account located within the Commonwealth, beyond the reach of the lessor's creditors.
A lessor holding a security deposit for one year or longer must pay interest at 5% per year (or the lesser amount actually earned) to the tenant annually.
The lessor must return the security deposit or balance thereof to the tenant within thirty days after termination of occupancy, subject to allowed deductions.

A lessor accepting a security deposit must furnish the tenant a written statement of the present condition of the premises, including a comprehensive listing of any existing damage, within specified timeframes.

A lessor forfeits the right to retain any portion of a security deposit if they fail to deposit funds properly, fail to provide itemized damage list, use conflicting lease provisions, fail to transfer deposit to successor, or fail to timely return the deposit.
If a lessor fails to comply with certain security deposit requirements, the tenant shall be awarded treble damages plus interest, court costs, and attorney's fees.
Fee in Lieu of Security Deposit Option is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
A security deposit continues to be the property of the tenant, cannot be commingled with lessor's assets, and is not subject to claims of the lessor's creditors.

No deduction may be made from the security deposit for any purpose other than those explicitly set forth in the statute, such as unpaid rent, unpaid tax escalation amounts, or damage caused by the tenant.
Any lease provision conflicting with the security deposit statute, or any tenant waiver of its provisions, is void and unenforceable as against public policy.

Landlords are prohibited from taking reprisals against tenants for reporting code violations, joining tenant unions, or exercising legal rights; receipt of a termination notice, rent increase, or substantial alteration of tenancy terms within six months of protected tenant activity creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of independent justification; any lease waiver of this protection is void.
Broker/Finder Fee Payment Restriction for Rental Housing is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

No person may engage in the business of finding dwelling accommodations for prospective tenants for a fee unless that person is a licensed broker or salesman as defined under section 87PP of chapter 112.

A landlord's written notice to quit for nonpayment of rent must be accompanied by a form containing documentation of repayment agreements, information on rental assistance programs, applicable court rules/orders on summary process, and relevant legal restrictions on evictions, along with a prominent statement informing the tenant that the notice is not an eviction and that only a court order can force them to leave. Courts may not accept eviction filings for nonpayment of rent without proof of delivery of this form.

The notice form must prominently display a statement informing tenants that a notice to quit is not an eviction, that they do not need to immediately leave, that they are entitled to a legal proceeding to defend against the eviction, and that only a court order can force them to leave.

No court with jurisdiction over summary process actions, including the Boston municipal court department, may accept for filing a writ, summons, or complaint in an eviction for nonpayment of rent for a residential dwelling unit without proof of delivery of the required notice-to-quit form.

A0234.explanation: It is unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley, and it is unlawful for a landlord to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels. Each month of violation per unit is a separate violation, enforceable via civil action by the City Attorney or an aggrieved tenant with civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation.

Prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making. It is unlawful to inquire about criminal history, indicate persons with criminal backgrounds will not be considered, refuse to rent or terminate tenancy based on criminal history, require disclosure of criminal history, demand higher deposits or rent based on criminal history, refuse to allow addition of family members based on criminal history, or disqualify tenants from rental assistance programs based on criminal history, subject to certain exemptions.
If a landlord takes any action against an applicant or tenant based on criminal history, the landlord is required to provide the applicant/tenant with written notice and an opportunity to respond.

Any landlord found to be in violation of the Ordinance shall be subject to administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages including actual damages or three times the amount of one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
2026 Relocation Assistance Payment Increase for Owner Move-In and Ellis Act Evictions is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
The maximum tenant screening fee landlords may charge prospective tenants in 2026 is $68.96.
Landlords cannot charge a prospective tenant a screening fee if no rental unit is actually available.
If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

The landlord must return a screening fee to any applicant not selected, or have a policy under which they review applications in the order received and the first qualified applicant gets the unit, and do not charge a screening fee to any applicant not considered.

When an owner charges a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application, the owner must provide a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under state law, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee.

An owner of residential rental property cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.

Chapter 13.78 applies to all residential rental agreements regardless of any contractual language in any rental agreement or lease to the contrary, and any provision of an existing rental agreement or lease that violates the provisions of this chapter are unenforceable.

The maximum Annual General Adjustment (AGA) that a landlord of a fully-covered rental unit may impose each year is capped at 5%, even if the Rent Ordinance formula would otherwise yield a higher percentage.
A landlord may not evict a tenant for nonpayment of rent unless the tenant owes rental debt equal to or greater than one month of the Fair Market Rent value for a unit of equivalent size.
A landlord cannot evict a tenant for failing to sign a substantially similar lease upon expiration of a fixed-term lease.

To evict a tenant for violation of a material lease term, the term must be mutually agreed upon, the violation must cause substantial, actual damage to the landlord, and the landlord must demonstrate the tenant's behavior was unreasonable.

The landlord must file with the Rent Board a copy of any notice to terminate a tenancy, notice to quit, and summons and complaint no later than three business days after the tenant was served with the document.
Landlords may only charge one month's rent as a security deposit for unfurnished and furnished units, starting July 1, 2024.

Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total can charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons.
Landlords must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy to identify any items that need repair or cleaning.
All or any remaining portion of a security deposit must be returned within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant, with an itemized statement of deductions if applicable.
Starting January 1, 2025, landlords must provide proof that necessary repairs were completed when making deductions from a security deposit.
Pre-Tenancy Photograph Requirement is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Post-Move-Out Photograph Requirement is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.
Eligible landlords may increase 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than January 1, 2026, with the increase equal to 65% of CPI change for the Bay Area from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025.
Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980 are fully covered by Berkeley's rent control, requiring registration and granting just cause eviction and security deposit interest protections.
Single family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996 are fully covered, including just cause eviction protections.
Rooming houses, defined as single-family homes with five or more rooms rented out individually with separate leases, are fully covered and subject to just cause eviction requirements.

New construction units that were built and received a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980 are partially covered, requiring registration and security deposit interest, though not subject to rent control or just cause eviction.
No Coverage for Golden Duplex Units is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

Housing providers may not consider certain categories of criminal history (arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged records, juvenile records) when screening applicants, and may not impose blanket bans on applicants with any criminal history.
Housing providers may not impose conditions that discriminate against households with children, including charging higher security deposits to families with children.
Housing providers may not charge higher security deposits or apply different terms based on an applicant's or tenant's source of income, such as Section 8 vouchers.
Tenants with service animals or emotional-support animals cannot be charged pet deposits or pet rent for those animals.

It is unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, or to coerce another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by a common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in California.

After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which must be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. Just cause includes at-fault reasons (e.g., nonpayment of rent, lease violations, nuisance, waste, criminal activity) and no-fault reasons (e.g., owner move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate, demolition or substantial remodel), with relocation assistance or rent waiver required for no-fault terminations.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, based on the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months, with no more than two increments over that period.
If the same tenant remains in occupancy over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period.

For a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the owner may establish the initial rental rate without the cap applying; the cap applies only to subsequent increases after that initial rate is set.

The rent cap does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories, housing subject to stricter local rent control, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome), certain single-family/condo properties meeting ownership and notice conditions, and owner-occupied duplexes.
An owner shall provide notice of any rent increase under subdivision (a) to each tenant in accordance with Section 827.
This section shall remain in effect until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.
A landlord shall not demand or receive security in an amount exceeding one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent, except as otherwise provided.
The one month's rent security deposit cap does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months' rent if the lease term is six months or longer.
Service Member Higher Security Disclosure is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

A landlord who is a natural person or LLC of natural persons owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units total may charge up to two months' rent as security deposit, unless the tenant is a service member.
Any security deposit shall be held by the landlord for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to the security has priority over any creditor of the landlord.
The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy, or for ordinary wear and tear.

The landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the right to request an initial inspection before move-out and must conduct the inspection upon tenant request, giving at least 48 hours' notice, to allow the tenant to remedy deficiencies before final deductions.
Photographs Required at Move-In is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Photographs Required at Move-Out is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated, the landlord shall furnish the tenant an itemized statement of deductions and return any remaining portion of the security deposit.
The landlord need not provide documentation for deductions if the deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed $125.

The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord of the security deposit in violation of this section may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security deposit as 'nonrefundable.'
Cap on Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Conditions for Charging Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

Landlords may not use a financial or income standard in rental housing that fails to account for the aggregate income of unmarried persons residing together on the same basis as married persons residing together.

When there is a government rent subsidy, landlords may not use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for rental housing that is not based on the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant.

When there is a government rent subsidy, a landlord using a person's credit history as part of the application process must offer the applicant the option to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their reasonable ability to pay the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant, such as government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements, and must reasonably consider that evidence in lieu of credit history.

If an applicant elects to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their ability to pay, the housing provider must provide the applicant reasonable time to respond with that alternative evidence and reasonably consider that alternative evidence in lieu of the person's credit history in determining whether to offer the rental accommodation to the applicant.

Annual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region, or 10%, whichever is lower, for buildings older than 15 years not otherwise exempt.
From August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable rent increase under AB 1482 is 8.9%.
State law requires landlords to provide 30 days' written advance notice of rent increases of less than 10%.

The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions lasting less than 20 days is governed by state law rather than the local Rent Ordinance provision covering longer displacements.

Prohibits termination of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions for most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO, once a tenant has lived in the unit for six months or their lease has expired.
Property owners who regain possession of a unit for reasons not the tenant's fault (e.g., owner move-in, demolition, conversion) may have to pay the tenant relocation assistance.
Landlords may not evict a tenant who falls behind in rent unless the tenant owes an amount higher than the Fair Market Rent (FMR) for the unit's bedroom size.

Annual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region, or 10%, whichever is lower, for buildings older than 15 years not otherwise exempt.
From August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable rent increase under AB 1482 is 8.9%.
Under the RSO, rent may be increased once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage set by LAHD.
As of February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer add an additional percentage increase for utilities on top of the allowable rent increase.
As of February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer charge an additional 10% rent increase for an additional dependent added to the tenancy.
A 10% rent increase is allowed for an additional tenant (not a dependent) who moves into a rental unit, and landlords can increase rent within 60 days of learning about the additional tenant.
All notices to terminate a tenancy for rental units subject to the RSO must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service on the tenant.
No-fault evictions require the landlord to pay tenant relocation assistance.
Landlords must give tenants 30-day and 60-day written notice for no-fault evictions, with some evictions requiring a 120-day notice or up to a 1-year extension.

Beginning August 20, 2025, landlords must post the Notice of Right to Counsel and provide it to the tenant at the start of the tenancy, and attach it to any eviction notice or termination of a rental subsidy.
The maximum annual rent increase for units subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance is 3% for the period July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026.
Elimination of Utility Surcharge Increase is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
State law requires landlords to provide 30 days' written advance notice of rent increases of less than 10%.
Effective January 1, 2022, landlords may collect a total SCEP fee of $67.94 per unit from tenants at a rate of $2.83 per month for 12 months each year, with proper written notice.
Effective January 1, 2020, landlords may collect a total RSO fee of $38.75 per unit from tenants at a rate of $1.61 per month for 12 months each year, with proper written notice.

In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction, and the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute just cause.

The landlord also needs a just cause reason to take away or remove access to certain housing services, including but not limited to garage facilities, parking facilities, driveways, storage spaces, and laundry rooms.

Some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limitations of the Ordinance, including newly constructed rental units with Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 and tenancies eligible for increases under Costa-Hawkins, are still subject to just cause eviction requirements.
For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is capped at 1.6%.

Prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco; allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action for violations.

The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions lasting less than 20 days is governed by state law rather than the local Rent Ordinance provision covering longer displacements.
Landlords subject to the San Francisco Rent Ordinance may increase rent by no more than 1.6% during the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
Landlords must pay tenants interest on security deposits at a rate of 4.2% for the period March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.

Landlords must pay relocation benefits to tenants evicted for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal of a unit from housing use, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation.
Landlords who evict tenants under the Ellis Act must pay relocation payments as set forth in the Rent Ordinance.
For temporary capital improvement evictions resulting in displacement of less than 20 days, relocation payments are governed by state law rather than the Rent Ordinance.

A0237.explanation: Landlords may only charge one month's rent as a security deposit for unfurnished and furnished units, starting July 1, 2024.

Landlords who own only two rental properties with no more than four residential units total can charge up to two months' rent if ownership is held by a natural person, family trust, or LLC where all members are natural persons.
Landlords must offer a walk-through inspection during the last two weeks of a tenancy to identify any items that need repair or cleaning.
All or any remaining portion of a security deposit must be returned within 21 days after the tenant leaves the unit vacant, with an itemized statement of deductions if applicable.
Starting January 1, 2025, landlords must provide proof that necessary repairs were completed when making deductions from a security deposit.

Housing providers may not consider certain categories of criminal history (arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged records, juvenile records) when screening applicants, and may not impose blanket bans on applicants with any criminal history.
Housing providers may not impose conditions that discriminate against households with children, including charging higher security deposits to families with children.
Housing providers may not charge higher security deposits or apply different terms based on an applicant's or tenant's source of income, such as Section 8 vouchers.
Tenants with service animals or emotional-support animals cannot be charged pet deposits or pet rent for those animals.

It is unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce, or to coerce another person to set or adopt a recommended price or commercial term recommended by a common pricing algorithm for the same or similar products or services in California.

After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which must be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy. Just cause includes at-fault reasons (e.g., nonpayment of rent, lease violations, nuisance, waste, criminal activity) and no-fault reasons (e.g., owner move-in, withdrawal from rental market, government order to vacate, demolition or substantial remodel), with relocation assistance or rent waiver required for no-fault terminations.

An owner of residential real property shall not increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or unit more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period, based on the lowest gross rental rate charged during the prior 12 months, with no more than two increments over that period.
If the same tenant remains in occupancy over any 12-month period, the gross rental rate shall not be increased in more than two increments over that 12-month period.

For a new tenancy in which no tenant from the prior tenancy remains in lawful possession, the owner may establish the initial rental rate without the cap applying; the cap applies only to subsequent increases after that initial rate is set.

The rent cap does not apply to deed-restricted affordable housing, dormitories, housing subject to stricter local rent control, housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome), certain single-family/condo properties meeting ownership and notice conditions, and owner-occupied duplexes.
An owner shall provide notice of any rent increase under subdivision (a) to each tenant in accordance with Section 827.
This section shall remain in effect until January 1, 2030, and as of that date is repealed.
A landlord shall not demand or receive security in an amount exceeding one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent, except as otherwise provided.
The one month's rent security deposit cap does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months' rent if the lease term is six months or longer.
Service Member Higher Security Disclosure is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

A landlord who is a natural person or LLC of natural persons owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units total may charge up to two months' rent as security deposit, unless the tenant is a service member.
Any security deposit shall be held by the landlord for the tenant, and the tenant's claim to the security has priority over any creditor of the landlord.
The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy, or for ordinary wear and tear.

The landlord must notify the tenant in writing of the right to request an initial inspection before move-out and must conduct the inspection upon tenant request, giving at least 48 hours' notice, to allow the tenant to remedy deficiencies before final deductions.
Photographs Required at Move-In is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Photographs Required at Move-Out is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated, the landlord shall furnish the tenant an itemized statement of deductions and return any remaining portion of the security deposit.
The landlord need not provide documentation for deductions if the deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed $125.

The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord of the security deposit in violation of this section may subject the landlord to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.
A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security deposit as 'nonrefundable.'
Cap on Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Conditions for Charging Application Screening Fees is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

Landlords may not use a financial or income standard in rental housing that fails to account for the aggregate income of unmarried persons residing together on the same basis as married persons residing together.

When there is a government rent subsidy, landlords may not use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for rental housing that is not based on the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant.

When there is a government rent subsidy, a landlord using a person's credit history as part of the application process must offer the applicant the option to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their reasonable ability to pay the portion of rent to be paid by the tenant, such as government benefit payments, pay records, and bank statements, and must reasonably consider that evidence in lieu of credit history.

If an applicant elects to provide lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of their ability to pay, the housing provider must provide the applicant reasonable time to respond with that alternative evidence and reasonably consider that alternative evidence in lieu of the person's credit history in determining whether to offer the rental accommodation to the applicant.

Annual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region, or 10%, whichever is lower, for buildings older than 15 years not otherwise exempt.
From August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable rent increase under AB 1482 is 8.9%.
State law requires landlords to provide 30 days' written advance notice of rent increases of less than 10%.

Prohibits termination of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions for most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO, once a tenant has lived in the unit for six months or their lease has expired.
Property owners who regain possession of a unit for reasons not the tenant's fault (e.g., owner move-in, demolition, conversion) may have to pay the tenant relocation assistance.
Landlords may not evict a tenant who falls behind in rent unless the tenant owes an amount higher than the Fair Market Rent (FMR) for the unit's bedroom size.

Annual rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region, or 10%, whichever is lower, for buildings older than 15 years not otherwise exempt.
From August 1, 2024 to July 31, 2025, the maximum allowable rent increase under AB 1482 is 8.9%.
Under the RSO, rent may be increased once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage set by LAHD.
As of February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer add an additional percentage increase for utilities on top of the allowable rent increase.
As of February 2, 2026, landlords may no longer charge an additional 10% rent increase for an additional dependent added to the tenancy.
A 10% rent increase is allowed for an additional tenant (not a dependent) who moves into a rental unit, and landlords can increase rent within 60 days of learning about the additional tenant.
All notices to terminate a tenancy for rental units subject to the RSO must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service on the tenant.
No-fault evictions require the landlord to pay tenant relocation assistance.
Landlords must give tenants 30-day and 60-day written notice for no-fault evictions, with some evictions requiring a 120-day notice or up to a 1-year extension.

Beginning August 20, 2025, landlords must post the Notice of Right to Counsel and provide it to the tenant at the start of the tenancy, and attach it to any eviction notice or termination of a rental subsidy.
The maximum annual rent increase for units subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance is 3% for the period July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026.
Elimination of Utility Surcharge Increase is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
State law requires landlords to provide 30 days' written advance notice of rent increases of less than 10%.
Effective January 1, 2022, landlords may collect a total SCEP fee of $67.94 per unit from tenants at a rate of $2.83 per month for 12 months each year, with proper written notice.
Effective January 1, 2020, landlords may collect a total RSO fee of $38.75 per unit from tenants at a rate of $1.61 per month for 12 months each year, with proper written notice.

The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions lasting less than 20 days is governed by state law rather than the local Rent Ordinance provision covering longer displacements.

A0239.explanation: It is unlawful to sell, license, or otherwise provide to City of Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in Berkeley, and it is unlawful for a landlord to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels. Each month of violation per unit is a separate violation, enforceable via civil action by the City Attorney or an aggrieved tenant with civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation.

Prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making. It is unlawful to inquire about criminal history, indicate persons with criminal backgrounds will not be considered, refuse to rent or terminate tenancy based on criminal history, require disclosure of criminal history, demand higher deposits or rent based on criminal history, refuse to allow addition of family members based on criminal history, or disqualify tenants from rental assistance programs based on criminal history, subject to certain exemptions.
If a landlord takes any action against an applicant or tenant based on criminal history, the landlord is required to provide the applicant/tenant with written notice and an opportunity to respond.

Any landlord found to be in violation of the Ordinance shall be subject to administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation, civil damages including actual damages or three times the amount of one month's rent, punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
2026 Relocation Assistance Payment Increase for Owner Move-In and Ellis Act Evictions is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
The maximum tenant screening fee landlords may charge prospective tenants in 2026 is $68.96.
Landlords cannot charge a prospective tenant a screening fee if no rental unit is actually available.
If the tenant provides a reusable screening report, the landlord must use it.

The landlord must return a screening fee to any applicant not selected, or have a policy under which they review applications in the order received and the first qualified applicant gets the unit, and do not charge a screening fee to any applicant not considered.

When an owner charges a fee to purchase a consumer credit report and to validate, review, or otherwise process an application, the owner must provide a clear and conspicuous tenant screening fee rights statement and a statement of the maximum fee cap permitted under state law, either in the rental application or in a separate disclosure before receiving the fee.

An owner of residential rental property cannot charge a non-refundable fee to any existing tenant for the purpose of renewing a tenancy, in whole or in part, including any fee associated with the departure of a roommate or to request to add or replace a roommate in a pre-existing household.

Chapter 13.78 applies to all residential rental agreements regardless of any contractual language in any rental agreement or lease to the contrary, and any provision of an existing rental agreement or lease that violates the provisions of this chapter are unenforceable.

The maximum Annual General Adjustment (AGA) that a landlord of a fully-covered rental unit may impose each year is capped at 5%, even if the Rent Ordinance formula would otherwise yield a higher percentage.
A landlord may not evict a tenant for nonpayment of rent unless the tenant owes rental debt equal to or greater than one month of the Fair Market Rent value for a unit of equivalent size.
A landlord cannot evict a tenant for failing to sign a substantially similar lease upon expiration of a fixed-term lease.

To evict a tenant for violation of a material lease term, the term must be mutually agreed upon, the violation must cause substantial, actual damage to the landlord, and the landlord must demonstrate the tenant's behavior was unreasonable.

The landlord must file with the Rent Board a copy of any notice to terminate a tenancy, notice to quit, and summons and complaint no later than three business days after the tenant was served with the document.

Pre-Tenancy Photograph Requirement is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.
Post-Move-Out Photograph Requirement is not yet effective on 2026-10-01.

For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.
Eligible landlords may increase 2025 permanent rent ceilings by 1.0% no earlier than January 1, 2026, with the increase equal to 65% of CPI change for the Bay Area from July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025.
Most units in multifamily properties built before 1980 are fully covered by Berkeley's rent control, requiring registration and granting just cause eviction and security deposit interest protections.
Single family homes with current tenancies that began before 1996 are fully covered, including just cause eviction protections.
Rooming houses, defined as single-family homes with five or more rooms rented out individually with separate leases, are fully covered and subject to just cause eviction requirements.

New construction units that were built and received a Certificate of Occupancy after June 1980 are partially covered, requiring registration and security deposit interest, though not subject to rent control or just cause eviction.

Cities and towns may not enact, maintain, or enforce rent control of any kind, except that a city or town may accept this chapter and adopt rent control regulation that meets specific conditions, including voluntary compliance after six months, exclusions for small property owners and higher-rent units, and a requirement that the municipality compensate owners from general funds for the difference between fair market rent and controlled rent.

After six months from the initial adoption of rent control regulation by a city or town, compliance by property owners is entirely voluntary, and property of an owner declining to participate is unaffected by the regulation.

Local rent control regulation may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion, or removal of properties from regulation, and may not apply to rental units owned by an owner with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent exceeding $400.

A municipality adopting rent control regulation must compensate owners of rent controlled units for the difference between the unit's fair market rent and its rent controlled rent, with such compensation paid from the municipality's general funds so that the cost is borne by all taxpayers rather than only the owners of regulated units.

Landlords and persons furnishing rental accommodations or credit may not discriminate against a prospective or current tenant because that person receives federal, state, or local public assistance (including medical assistance) or receives federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements, nor may they discriminate because of any requirement of such assistance or subsidy program.

A landlord may terminate a tenancy for nonpayment of rent by giving fourteen days' written notice to quit, unless the tenant pays or tenders all rent due, with interest and costs, before the answer is due in a possession action.

If nonpayment of rent was caused by delay in a government subsistence or rental payment, the court must continue the hearing at least seven days to notify the agency, and must treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent, interest, and costs are tendered within that time.

Tenancies at will may be terminated by either party with three months' written notice, or if rent is paid at intervals of less than three months, notice equal to the payment interval or thirty days, whichever is longer. For nonpayment of rent, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient, unless the tenant has not received similar notice in the preceding twelve months, in which case the tenant may cure by paying all rent due within ten days of receipt of the notice. Notices for nonpayment must include a statutory notification of the tenant's right to cure.

In case of neglect or refusal to pay rent due, fourteen days' written notice to quit is sufficient to terminate a tenancy at will, unless the tenant has not received a similar notice within the preceding twelve months and pays or tenders the full amount of rent due within ten days after receipt of the notice.

Every notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent must contain a specific notification informing the tenant of their right to prevent termination by paying the full amount of rent due within ten days of receipt, if they have not received such a notice within the preceding twelve months.

If a notice to determine an estate at will for nonpayment of rent fails to contain the required statutory notification, the tenant's time to pay or tender rent is extended to the day the answer is due in any action by the landlord to recover possession of the premises.

If neglect or refusal to pay rent was caused by a delay in mailing or delivery of a subsistence or rental payment by a government entity, the court must continue the hearing for at least seven days to notify the appropriate agency, and shall treat the tenancy as not terminated if all rent due, with interest and costs, is tendered to the landlord within that time.
A lessor may not require a security deposit exceeding the first month's rent, provided the deposit is held as required and a statement of condition is given to the tenant.
